content.thinking:
I'm planning out the design for a chunky, Blizzard-style gray wolf model—oversized head, shoulders, and paws with a painted look, roughly 0.8m at the shoulder and 1.9m total length including tail. I want to write the full file carefully in one pass without testing, keeping API calls minimal, with the model facing +Z and left being +X.

Now I'm sketching out the skeleton hierarchy: a hip root joint, a spine chain built from catmull-rom points running from hips through the mid-back to the chest/withers, then a two-span neck chain rising up to a head joint, each parented to the appropriate preceding joint in the chain.

I'm reconsidering the body sweep itself, extending the spine path to include a rump section behind the hips so the torso silhouette reads as a full wolf body rather than stopping abruptly at the hip joint.

Now I'm shaping the body's cross-section radii along its length -- narrower rump, deepening through the mid-body, and a prominent deep chest near the front before tapering slightly at the neck base -- while checking that the resulting chest depth still leaves room for the front legs to reach the ground naturally.

For color, I'm defining a hand-painted wolf palette (dark and light grays, cream belly, black, brown, nose black, amber eyes) and building a countershaded mottled coat texture blending grainy gray tones on top with a creamier underside, rather than using a flat toon-cel style.

Writing paint function for saddle...

Now I'm working out the front leg geometry: shoulder joint position, then a multi-segment limb through elbow, wrist, and down to the paw target, checking that the summed segment lengths roughly match the distance to the foot.

Still defining paw geometry and the leg chain hierarchy, naming joints as shoulder/elbow/wrist/paw for the front leg, parented correctly to the spine with a side attribute. Now I'm moving to the hind leg, mapping hip/thigh/stifle/hock joints and figuring out which spine joint should parent the hip.

Setting front and hind foot targets, then working out leg sweep radii tapering from thigh to paw for both front and hind limbs, plus adding haunch bulk spheres on the hip bones for volume.

For leg coloring I'm planning a gradient that darkens toward the lower legs, with a darker front-leg stripe like real wolves have, binding each paw sweep to its nearest joint so the geometry follows the rig correctly.

Now I'm designing the tail as a drooping curved chain hanging down from the hips, tapering from a bushy root to a pointed tip, with the coat color fading to dark near the end through a gradient along the tail's path.

I'm also adding fur tuft cards for texture on the neck ruff, cheeks, and tail -- using simple grey SVG shapes with slightly darker streak lines that get tinted by the coat color paint, giving a sense of individual tufts without full 3D geometry. The tail tip sits comfortably above the floor, so nothing clips.

Now I'm working out the head attachment and orientation, setting up a local coordinate helper so I can position head parts using forward/up/left offsets relative to the head joint, being careful about which axis corresponds to the model's left versus right side. With that in place, I start building out the skull itself -- making it oversized to fit Blizzard's big-wolf proportions, beginning with a scaled cranium sphere positioned using those local offsets.

Writing muzzle geometry...

Still defining the muzzle sweep shape, then placing a small nose sphere and planning triangular ear shapes positioned on the head using sharp-cornered extrusions.

I'm reconsidering the ear geometry—simplifying to draw the outline flat in the X-Y plane with thickness extruded along Z, so the shape is perpendicular and easier to reason about, then adding outward lean by skewing the outline points themselves rather than tilting the extrusion axis.

Now I'm positioning the inner ear with a pinkish-grey tint and thickness, then placing the eyes as small amber spheres with black slit pupils on the skull surface near where the muzzle begins, checking that their position stays within the muzzle's cross-section at that forward distance.

Working out brow ridge placement and eye details — adding a darker capsule for the brow spike, then positioning iris and pupil spheres so the pupil sits just outside the iris surface for an alert look.

Adding a tiny white highlight sphere for eye shine, then planning small dark spheres along the upper lip for whisker spots and cheek/forehead details.

Now I'm figuring out the face mask paint logic using world-space coordinates relative to the head's position, since the head sits around z .8–1.15 in rest pose. I'm setting up conditions based on surface normals and offsets from the head reference point to paint a dark nose bridge stripe and define lip shading boundaries.

Then I'm layering cheek shading and defaulting to a countershaded grey-cream mottle for the rest of the face, so the paint function returns distinct colors depending on normal direction and vertical position, with the bridge dark stripe and cream underside taking priority before falling back to the general mottled base. Now I'm shifting to work on the neck geometry, planning a swept chain shape with a tapering radius.

Mapping out the neck-to-head transition...

Filtering the sweep to the lower belly region, then planning card counts for different fur zones — neck, body, chest ruff, tail, cheeks — keeping triangle counts manageable per card with simple bends. I'll apply vertex-painted coat color and a separate gradient tint pass for the tail, scattering each region's cards as its own call.

For the back I'm adding a darker saddle crest using height and position filters, then writing a paint function that blends grey tones with noise and smoothstep masks to darken the spine region relative to the belly's countershading.

Now I'm adding anisotropic noise streaks for fur texture, then setting the belly to a cream-and-grey mottled pattern and combining both via countershading. I'm also tuning the body proportions toward chunky Blizzard-style traits — oversized head, thick shoulders, and large paws.

Still working out body part placement...

I'll skip the precise dark lip line for now and focus on bigger decisions: keeping the design natural without collars or war paint, maybe adding ragged ear notches and fur tufts on the hind legs. I'm checking that paw and toe sweeps sit close enough to the floor without clipping, and estimating overall head height with cranium and ears stacking up to around 1.3 units, matching a realistic wolf proportion.

I'm now rescaling the whole body for believability -- shoulder height around 0.85, neck curve points leading to the head, and ear height trimmed down to 0.16 so the total height lands near 1.24 meters, a bit oversized but fitting a chunky stylized wolf. Checking body length from nose to tail tip gives roughly 2.3 meters, slightly larger than a real wolf but acceptable, and now I'm cross-checking leg segment lengths against the shoulder height for proportional consistency.

I'm figuring out the taper of the body cross-section along the spine -- blending a wider chest radius near the front with a narrowing rump toward the back using smoothstep functions for both the x and y radii, then rounding off the end caps so the final radius at the tail tip comes out to about 0.165.

I'm also adding a downward shift near the chest to simulate a hanging belly, computed as a function returning a vertical offset based on the chest smoothstep weight, and checking that the rump's top edge lines up around y=.93 so the haunch sphere fits cleanly. Now I'm noting that the legs will use a coat-gradient paint, matching the shoulders, and planning to add chest ruff details and ear geometry next.

Now I'm figuring out the ordering constraints for building the mesh: joints and chains need to exist before sweeps, parts, and surface cards are generated, and the head geometry has to be built after its joint with a slight tilt direction applied locally. I'm working out how front leg limbs are generated from a root vector near the shoulder, with joint names suffixed by side (L/R) and parented to the correct spine joint, and double-checking the chain path array structure for each limb.

For the leg bones I'm deciding between polyline (sharp joints, smoothed later by the sweep fillet) versus catmull (naturally smooth through points but risks drifting off the exact limb endpoints) — leaning toward polyline since sweeping will round the corners anyway. I'm also verifying that the hind leg chain parents to the correct hip joint since it sits at the same position as the body's hip socket, and working out the limb bend plane and hint vector for the front elbow so it bends backward correctly.

Now I'm setting up matching knee/hock bend directions for the hind legs, then designing the paw geometry: a sphere for the paw pad, three toe spheres with offset positions, and small dark claw spikes at the tips with their own length, radius, and base position. I'm also sketching out a darker leg coat gradient to mimic the tan/black lower-leg coloring on a wolf.

For the legs and paws, I'm reusing that leg-coat color for the paw spheres, scattering some fur tuft cards on the back of the front legs for texture, and now I'm starting to plot the tail's control points as a chain parented to the hips, beginning at the root near the rear of the body and curving downward and outward.

I'm setting a tapering radius array for the tail sweep so it narrows to a point at the tip, and planning a gradient paint that darkens toward the end along with a dark stripe running along the top of the tail for a more realistic look. Now moving on to assign the tail segments to the bone chain.

Tallying up the full skeleton joint count across hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, legs, and tail, I'm making sure I give every part an explicit color since I never want anything defaulting to grey. I'm double-checking my imports stay strict-TS-safe with nothing unused, considering whether to add a subtle glow effect to the eyes with amber iris color, and sketching out the meta object with name, description, style, and commit info.

For painted shadow shading in the Blizzard style, I'm layering warm rim light and top-gradient lightening on top of the countershading already in place, then moving into writing the actual implementation, pulling in the Joint type from skeleton.ts and setting up a head helper function that converts local offsets into model-space points.

I realize the local-to-world conversion uses model directions rather than bone-relative ones, so I'll keep the head tilt subtle and consistent. Now I'm defining helper functions for building head parts—spheres, extrusions, and capsules for eyebrows—with small segment counts and thin extrude settings for bevels and thickness.

Positioning the eyebrow slightly above the eye height, then adding scattered cheek ruff cards on the cranium surface filtered by position and normal direction to keep them on the sides. I'm also considering a nose sphere, skipping nostril detail, and adding a dark capsule line for the lower lip along the jaw.

Actually that capsule position falls inside the muzzle rather than on its surface, so it'd be hidden—I'll skip the capsule and instead paint a dark lip color using a normal-based condition to target the lower muzzle side.

I also need cream fur coloring on the lower muzzle and jaw via normal-direction thresholds, since the head paint function covers cranium, muzzle, and jaw together. For the ears, I'm defining colors too: dark grey on the back, pinkish inner, with a darker tip painted based on vertical position within the extrusion.

Now I'm building the spine chain using a catmull curve through the hip, mid-back, and shoulder points, naming three spine joints to match the three spans, then sweeping the body mesh along that chain with a radius profile that varies with position along the path.

Next I'm placing the haunch and shoulder sphere parts bound to their leg joints, then scattering fur tufts and card clusters along each leg's sweep surface, filtering by normal direction and tuning their size, lean, and bend parameters for a natural coat look.

Moving on to the tail, chest ruff, and back crest, I'm scattering card clusters over their sweep surfaces with filters on surface height and normal to control where fur flows, picking density, size, lean, and bend values to match a backward-and-downward growth pattern.
